segments.text: The Sale of Goods Act regulates contracts in which ownership in goods is transferred or agreed to be transferred for a price.

Focus on when property and risk pass, the difference between a completed sale and an agreement to sell, quality/title obligations, buyer/seller remedies and unpaid-seller rights. Caveat emptor means buyer beware subject to recognized exceptions; nemo dat concerns transfer of title by a person who does not own it.
Primary authority: Sale of Goods Act, 1930, current official text.

The Sale of Goods Act, 1930 regulates contracts in which property in goods is transferred or agreed to be transferred for a price. A sale transfers ownership at the legally relevant time, while an agreement to sell contemplates a future or conditional transfer. This distinction affects risk, remedies and what happens if a party becomes insolvent.
Always separate ownership from possession. A buyer may possess goods before ownership passes, or ownership may pass while delivery is still pending.

A condition goes to the root of the contract in the statutory sense, while a warranty is a collateral stipulation whose breach normally supports damages rather than rejection. The Act also implies important terms concerning title, correspondence with description or sample and, in defined circumstances, quality or fitness.
Caveat emptor—let the buyer beware—is therefore not absolute. The statute allocates risk through express terms, implied terms and exceptions designed to protect legitimate reliance.

blocks.text: Transfer of title and unpaid seller

segments.text: The nemo dat principle means a person generally cannot transfer a better title than he possesses, subject to statutory exceptions that protect particular commercial transactions. Questions on title should identify the seller’s authority, possession, representations and any relevant exception.

An unpaid seller may have rights against the goods and personal remedies against the buyer. Lien, stoppage in transit and resale must be kept conceptually distinct because they arise in different factual situations.

items.text: A sale of goods is not merely a contract to deliver something; it concerns transfer or agreed transfer of property in goods for a price. The timing of transfer matters for rights and risk.
A sale transfers ownership immediately according to the legal rules; an agreement to sell contemplates a future or conditional transfer. This distinction affects remedies and risk in important ways.
Conditions are fundamental contractual terms; warranties are subsidiary terms. Breach produces different legal consequences, although statute may allow particular treatment in specified situations.
Caveat emptor means the buyer ordinarily bears responsibility for choice, but statutory exceptions protect buyers where reliance, description, quality obligations or other conditions apply.

Nemo dat protects ownership by limiting the title a non-owner can pass, subject to statutory exceptions. Unpaid-seller rights should be divided into rights against the goods and personal rights against the buyer.

rows: Common confusion to avoid: Do not memorize “buyer beware” as an absolute rule. The Act contains important exceptions and implied obligations.

items.text: Prepare conditions vs warranties with consequences of breach.
Study unpaid seller rights against goods and against buyer separately.
